newsitem.title: CONGO: French troops start leaving Congo, fresh clashes.
newsitem.headline: French troops start leaving Congo, fresh clashes.

text.p: France began pulling its troops out of the Congo Republic capital on Monday and the warring parties exchanged fire once again despite peace talks in Gabon.
French military spokesman Colonel Henry Pelissier said that 306 of the 1,200 or so French troops in Brazzaville left on Monday for Chad or Gabon on board 16 flights.

France is pressing ahead with the withdrawal despite an appeal from Congo President Pascal Lissouba that it leave troops in the city as a buffer force between the army and militiamen loyal to his rival, former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.
"Our priority is pulling out. Until the end we will keep the means to intervene if necessary with an armoured capacity," Pelissier told reporters.
The conflict began when the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home in a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the run-up to a presidential election scheduled for July 27.
The death toll from the fighting could run into hundreds, or even thousands according to some sources.
Troops loyal to Lissouba and militiamen loyal to Sassou Nguesso exchanged rocket fire and mortar and rocket-propelled grenades on Monday afternoon from opposing sides of the international airport.

Witnesses said Lissouba loyalists also fired rockets in the direction of Sassou Nguesso's forces in their stronghold in the northern suburbs. Sassou Nguesso loyalists took territory from Lissouba loyalists earlier in the conflict.
"We telephoned the two sides and told them that (their fire) was passing over the runway," Pelissier said. "They stopped and I think they understood the rules of the game," he added.

The French troops initially went to the city as part of a Western operation to evacuate foreign nationals from Kinshasa in the event of a bloodbath at the end of the civil war in former Zaire. It never occurred.
French troops have evacuated 5,719 foreign nationals, 1,544 of them French citizens, but France is still keeping its embassy open.
France called on Monday for the election to go ahead. "An immediate return to democracy via a presidential election is essential to the future of Congo," its Foreign Ministry said.
Lissouba says the election should take place as planned. Sassou Nguesso has called for guarantees of transparency, fairness and security first.
Lissouba has called for an African peace force, an idea which Sassou Nguesso has not ruled out.
In Gabon's capital Libreville the presidents of Gabon, Chad, Mali and Central African Republic held bilateral talks with Congolese mediators and representatives of the warring parties.
All sides were due to meet for a mini-summit to broker an end to the ethnic and political clashes. Mediators said deployment of an African force was on the agenda.
The two rivals declared a truce on Wednesday but some Western analysts fear the battle will ignite around the city's international airport once French troops leave.
